$TSM $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE TAIWAN OCTOBER SALES: RECORDS ACROSS THE CHAIN

All 34 tracked companies have now reported October revenue. Aggregate NT$3,739.2B, up 6.9% month on month after a mixed September. Every company grew year on year and the median gain was about 47%. The month set records up and down the chain: an all-time high at TSMC, an all-time high at Foxconn, a twelfth straight monthly record at Nanya, a fourth straight record at Global Unichip. The AI hardware chain did not just grow into the fourth quarter. It accelerated.

THE MACRO CHECK

Taiwan's own trade data says the same thing. October exports hit a record $96.76 billion, up 58.9% year on year, the first month ever above $90 billion and the thirty-sixth straight month of year-on-year growth. Integrated circuit exports were NT$1.02 trillion. Imports also set a record, and semiconductor equipment imports rose 83.4% year on year to $4.92 billion: capacity is still being built, not harvested. The Ministry of Finance expects demand to stay strong through the fourth quarter, with geopolitics and US trade policy named as the risks.

FOUNDRY

TSMC printed the biggest month in its history: NT$586,890M, up 59.7% year on year and 14.7% month on month, about $17.9 billion. It topped August's previous record by NT$72 billion, was the first month above NT$550 billion and the third straight above NT$500 billion. Revenue for the first ten months, NT$4,485.6B, already exceeds the whole of 2025. TSMC gave no breakdown, but the guide math is informative: fourth-quarter guidance of $52.3 to $54.3 billion needs November and December to average roughly NT$538 to $570 billion, below October's pace. The guide embeds a sequential step-down from the October run rate, which leaves room to beat it. Management's recent framing is that output may fall short of demand in coming quarters. The constraint is supply, not orders.

Behind TSMC, the mature-node names confirm the shape: UMC up 18.3% year on year and flat on the month, steady rather than accelerating. Powerchip rose 94.2% year on year on the DRAM rebound. Vanguard VIS fell 20.2% on the month after rising 15.9% in September, 8-inch lumpiness with the trend intact at +20.5% year on year. This is a leading-edge cycle.

MEMORY

Nanya rose 487.7% year on year to a twelfth consecutive monthly record, and Winbond rose 257.0%. The detail that matters: this supercycle is price, not volume. Nanya's third-quarter selling prices rose about 60% in a single quarter while bit shipments fell by a mid-single-digit percentage, producing a gross margin of 85.7%. In October its shipments dipped again after it exhausted available inventory, while prices kept rising. Management expects prices to rise further in the fourth quarter, and AI infrastructure is now more than 20% of its revenue. The module makers confirm the NAND side: Phison up 346.3% year on year to a record, ADATA up 282.3%.

The one caution in the memory tape is the same as last month: Nanya and Winbond grew only 3 to 4% month on month. Levels are still rising, but the rate of change has likely peaked.

Musings of the Day, 11/11/26:

Many are pointing to $CRWV’s prepaid deals as proof the DEBT GOVERNOR doesn’t bind AI compute. I’d respectfully submit the opposite.

1. Management’s own words: “We will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields.” That IS the Debt Governor talking. Cash interest hit $846M for the quarter, up from $310M a year ago, which is how a 62% Adj. EBITDA margin still became a $709M net loss.

2. The prepays are carrying the cash flow statement. Operating cash flow was $1.98B, while deferred revenue rose $2.13B. Strip out customers paying upfront and operations burned cash. A prepay is a LOAN from the customer, repaid in compute.

3. So who’s lending? OpenAI (funded by equity and increasingly debt) and the Hyperscalers, who’ve gone from funding ~9% of capex with new debt in 2024 to ~32% today. The Debt Governor didn’t disappear. It moved to the balance sheets writing the checks.

4. Customers only prepay when capacity is SCARCE. Hyperscalers with cheap IG capital and paid-off fleets use neoclouds as overflow in a boom and keep their own data centers full in a bust. If end demand merely grows slower than expected, the prepays vanish first, and the Bullwhip snaps hardest on the leveraged supplier furthest UPSTREAM -- like $CRWV.

The Tell: watch the share of deals that still come with prepays. When that fades while Hyperscaler borrowing keeps climbing, Credit is your Canary in the Coalmine.

直接体现市场对于算力的供需冷暖“鸭先知”。现在市场对于算力需求爆棚，谁能先上线当然短期合同租金高涨，快速回本。和酒店在旺季提价一个道理

现在最新财报再一次证明算力需求的紧缺时期，从不断上涨的租金，7层需求都是已经有客户提前预付款，财富500强10%采购渗透。

这个至少短期极高的算力需求对于上游芯片存储互联都是利好和证据。而且也缓解市场普遍认为公司融资风险，还有就是老的GPU价值还在涨价

当然建设风险就是“融资提款在前、通电收费在后”的时间错配风险，是市场主要担心民主党所在。我也周报分析了，AI经济发展需要规范而不可能扼杀。这个是对选票负责，无论什么党。而且需求在，新建供给压缩，反而利好现有的租金

其他比如软件服务方面都是锦上添花。核心看着这种股票投资价值所在

典型的概念和期权性质股票，风险承受力高的可以考虑，分析这个股票价值，在于验证AI泡沫的程度。

具体颗粒度更细的对于新云公司的行业解读和投资策略估值区间见订阅者时间线搜索

当然如果只出租GPU，归根到底就是高杠杆、强周期、硬件快速折旧的数据中心运营商，不同在于AI爆发性的算力需求。

它们用客户合同和预付款证券化未来算力需求，用融资购买电力、GPU 和时间，再通过集群软件把硬件转化成有效 Token。

短期利润来自稀缺高租金，长期价值则取决于能否从 GPU 小时收费升级为 Token、软件和工作流收费。

如果升级失败，它们最终只是高杠杆、强周期的数据中心运营商。如果升级成功，它们将成为介于英伟达、云大厂和 AI 应用之间的新型第三方算力提供商模式

当然它的成功就是英伟达的成功，避免被人家说什么循环融资，英伟达也不希望任何单一云厂商控制 AI 算力入口，特别是云大厂现在也搞自研的芯片。

CUSTOMER-FUNDED COMPONENT INVENTORY IMPROVES JABIL’S EXPOSURE TO THE AI BUILDOUT (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected company: Jabil Inc. (JBL: US). Direction: positive. Magnitude: meaningful program-level opportunity and favorable working-capital protection; the incremental consolidated earnings contribution remains undisclosed.

The decisive supplier connection appears in Akamai’s September contractual disclosure. Jabil was authorized to purchase approximately $1.7 billion of memory components, with Akamai paying the corresponding supplier invoices when Jabil receives the components. Pending use, Jabil holds the inventory on consignment for Akamai and repurchases it at cost as it is consumed in production.

The transmission mechanism is therefore more attractive than a generic increase in contract-manufacturing orders. Akamai funds the advance component stockpile, reducing Jabil’s exposure to carrying that inventory during the interval before server assembly. Jabil retains manufacturing, integration, warranty, spare-parts, and repair opportunities without necessarily financing the entire early procurement requirement. This structure transfers an important portion of the inventory-financing burden toward the infrastructure owner.

The $1.7 billion authorization is equivalent to approximately 4.7% of Jabil’s roughly $36 billion fiscal 2026 revenue, demonstrating the program’s scale. It is not evidence of $1.7 billion of immediate incremental Jabil revenue, nor should Jabil’s corporate operating margin be applied to that amount. Component pass-through, consignment accounting, manufacturing fees, and shipment acceptance determine the actual revenue and profit contribution.

22 months ago, we published the below analysis raising concerns that Nvidia's AI chips were potentially being routed to China through Singapore.

At the time, in the previous 3 quarters, $17.4 billion of Nvidia's revenue came from Singapore versus $11.6 billion from China.

We insist that our partners comply with all applicable laws, and if we receive any information to the contrary, act accordingly. Our last 10-Q noted: 'most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant.'"

Fast forward to today.

Nvidia maintains that it has no reason to believe US national security or company secrets were compromised.

"They're not, because they are synthetic exposures. They're derivatives of the shares in different shapes and forms, depending on who is doing it."

"These derivatives are issued offshore. They're not registered in the US. They're not compliant with US laws, for the most part. They don't necessarily pass the rights in terms of dividends or voting or things like that."

"I think the innovation exemption explicitly mentioned that synthetic exposure is not allowed in the US."

All Rallies are Opportunities to Sell:
When I build portfolios, I am constantly looking for good ideas. Some of them turn out to be not so good of ideas. When big rallies come, they are opportunities to dump all those bad ideas onto an eager buyer at much higher prices. When the big rallies come, I fade my lowest conviction stocks first even if its a small loss. A small loss in a bad investment is much better than a big loss at a bottom. 

All crashes are Opportunities to Buy:
Any selloff is an chance to add to core positions at cheaper prices and build upon the companies that survived the last rally due to high quality and performance. Its also a time to add companies I found from doing research from my watch list. 

Too many investors sell winners to throw good money after bad into their losers. I do the opposite. I sell losers into rallies so I can buy more of my winners into crashes.

quoted.text:
The math is fine. The accounting is wrong.

When a fund pays out 11%, its price drops by that amount. That's not income. It's a withdrawal with less control over taxes and timing than selling shares yourself.

What matters is total return. If the fund earns 6% and pays 11%, you're eating 5% of your principal every year. The "paycheck" shrinks each year and inflation and taxes make it worse. Those yields usually come from covered calls or return of capital, which cap your upside and leave you with the downside. 

Take the popular "distribution Yield" funds for example. QQQI sells call options on the Nasdaq 100. That premium is the "income," but it means handing someone else your gains above a certain level. You keep the downside and give up part of the upside thinking you got safer "income" when you actually locked in a lower total return. 

And the upside is where stock returns come from, usually in a few sharp rallies after selloffs. In April 2026 alone, QQQ returned about 15.7% to QQQI's 10.3%. Add a 0.68% fee versus 0.18% for QQQ and it falls further behind. It wins in flat markets, but the longer you hold the longer you give up the compound upside trend. 

Here's the actual "paycheck" result using the OP example. Both accounts paid out the exact same paychecks on the exact same days. The one that "sold shares" just has more left because it didn't pay the high fees or cap its upside with covered call "income".

posts.text:
Here's my 16" OLED MacBook Pro review after using it for the last few days:

• The OLED display is the best display I've ever seen on any consumer phone, TV or laptop. It's much brighter than my previous M1 Max Mini LED MacBook Pro Display. I've always been an insane person who likes to have the screen brightness at max output, but this is the first time where I feel like I don’t want to do that because its so bright. While a lot of people focus on peak HDR brightness (this can hit 2,000 nits), I'm more appreciative of the 67% higher sustained SDR brightness, because that's what you're using most to the time. My M1 got 600 nits sustained. The OLED gets 1,000.

• The speakers are noticeably better. The 50% deeper bass is great, but it's really the tweeters that sound much better. The clarity is improved, and they sound less tin like. The sound stage also feels wider.

• The 15% lighter weight is noticeable, very noticeable. My laptop no longer feels like a tank lol. This will be especially nice when traveling.

• Space Black is really just dark gray. Can we get an actual black laptop?

• While I’m not using the touchscreen a lot, I find myself using it more than I thought I would. It’s one of those things that’s nice to have when you need it, but you likely won’t need it much.

• I like that the glowing Apple logo is back, but can we get some stats on how much battery it uses? And why is this a feature that we can’t easily turn off in settings? I know it can be done, but it requires too many complicated steps.

• The M5 Max chip is awesome. Way better than my previous 2021 M1 Max MacBook Pro that I’m upgrading from. But it’s kind of a bummer that this new OLED MacBook Pro uses the same chips that came out early this year. M7 Pro and M7 Max are rumored to be added in late 2027, which should be a huge leap.

• I love the Dynamic Island. Much better than the notch because it’s actually useful. I find myself controlling media from it quite frequently.

• The OLED one has a curved display on the bottom vs squared off for the previous MacBook Pro, and this seems minor, but it does give the whole display a softer, more uniform look.

• Lastly, the lid opening notch’s pointy edges are way too sharp. They’re so sharp that it almost hurts to rest my thumbs there. Apple should round those off a bit so they’re smoother.

The OLED display and lighter weight alone are worth the extra $400 vs the Mini-LED MacBook Pro in my opinion. Fantastic laptop.

Despite the poor technical condition of the major indexes, a surprising number of sound setups are progressing across traditional growth sectors. The disconnect is unmistakable: select growth stocks are showing promise, but the broader market continues to deteriorate. Until participation broadens meaningfully, the foundation for a sustainable advance simply isn't there.

I remain 100% in cash. A follow-through day accompanied by broadening, healthy leadership would warrant a change in stance. Ex-Tesla President Jon McNeill reveals Elon Musk's idea for Neuralink started in the back of a Model S in Hong Kong, with Elon asking how fast he could type.

Elon Musk then asked for the top brain-computer interface researchers’ papers on the spot, and met them the next week:

“Elon and I were traveling together to China. We just landed in Hong Kong. We’re in the back of a Model S, and we’re both catching up on our inbox on our phones. And he looks over at me and says, how fast can you type with your thumbs?”

“And I said, I have no idea. I’ve never timed it. He’s like, well, the average human’s 18 words a minute. He said, how fast can you type on a keyboard? I said, I think it’s like 60 or 70 words a minute. So let’s call it 60.”

“He said, exactly. So you are more than three times faster on the keyboard than you are on your phone. This device has slowed the input into the machine. And he’s like, that’s a big deal, because you can’t get speed of answers and decision making if you’re going three times slower.”

“He’s like, what if you could think into the machine? I was like, well, that would blow this constraint away, because now we don’t have keyboards and thumbs to go through. You’re thinking in real time into the machine. He’s like, exactly. That would pull the front-end constraint off of the compute for humans. That’s a big deal.”

“So he didn’t sit on these ideas. He’s very unique in this way. And he said to his chief of staff, Sam Teller, who’s in the front seat: Sam, can you track down the top neuro computer science interface researchers in the world? Get their papers.”

“I want to read the papers while we’re here in China and on the flight back, and I want to meet with these people next week, because I want to start to work on brain-computer interface. And just like that, fast.”

“So by the next week, he’s meeting with some of the top minds in the world on this topic, and he doesn’t let go until he starts Neuralink.”

Inflation is driven by four primary mechanisms that reduce purchasing power across the economy: 

1. Monetary expansion. Excessive currency creation by central banks or governments increases the money supply faster than economic output, lowering the value of each dollar. 

2. Demand-pull pressure. Consumer, business, or government spending grows faster than the available supply of goods and services, prompting sellers to raise prices. 

3. Cost-push increases. Rising production expenses: such as higher costs for raw materials, energy, or supply chain inputs, force businesses to pass those added costs on to consumers. 

4. Built-in inflation. Shared expectations of future price increases lead workers to demand higher wages and companies to preemptively raise prices, creating a self-reinforcing cycle.

The Democratic midterm sweep has raised valid questions about the AI data centre buildout. The reality is more nuanced than the recent market reaction suggests.

2027 capacity looks largely intact. Most projects scheduled to come online next year are already under construction and newly elected governors are not expected to disrupt work that has started. Hyperscaler capex forecasts for 2027 remain essentially unchanged.

The risk sits further out. Roughly 20% of planned US capacity for 2028 (about 5 GW) could slip into 2029, mainly in Texas and Ohio, as new permitting and utility rules are written. This creates a potential air pocket for parts of the supply chain in 2028, but it is a delay not a cancellation.

Power constraints and interconnection queues were already going to push some projects later. Politics is now an additional variable, not the sole driver.
